voiceover.text: So, what can one community learn from another? A program improved children's health in one town. Another town copied it exactly, and nothing happened. Write down four reasons that could explain it. Then rank them, most likely first.

scenes.title: the syllabus example, as a model

voiceover.text: In Year 11 you localised the goals: start from a local need, and act across the Ottawa action areas. The syllabus names one body that did this: Healthy Cities Illawarra. Treat it as a model, not a list of projects. Since 1987, it has been a community-based organisation working on the conditions that produce health, not on treating illness. It works by convening, bringing councils, health services, schools, businesses and community groups together on local priorities. Its work maps onto the four goals. Food security, activity and social connection are SDG 3. School programs and helping people take part are SDG 4. Focusing on groups usually left out is SDG 10. And walking and cycling routes, community gardens and speaking up in planning decisions are SDG 11. One body, working on all four, because a community's problems don't arrive sorted by goal. So what transfers isn't any single project. It's having an independent, local, long-lasting body whose job is to hold the connections between sectors.

scenes.title: what keeps appearing: your checklist, plus two lines

voiceover.text: Across successful community approaches, the same features keep appearing, and five are already on your strategy checklist. The community sets the priority, not just commenting on a plan already written. It works across sectors, because health alone can't change housing, transport or food. It changes conditions, not just behaviour. A footpath keeps working when the campaign stops. It lasts long enough, because conditions built over a decade won't shift in a two-year project. And it measures, by group. Two features are new lines. It works in settings people already use, like schools, workplaces and clubs. And it builds local capacity, so skills stay when funding ends. The usual barrier isn't willingness. It's funding. Short, competitive grants push groups toward small, visible projects and away from the slow work that changes outcomes.

scenes.title: four more approaches, and the mechanism in each

voiceover.text: Four more patterns, each with its mechanism. Community-controlled health services are run by the communities they serve. Care designed by the people using it feels safe, so it's used, and chronic conditions get managed early. School programs reach every child without a family having to seek anything out. Whole-of-town food and activity changes alter what's on offer, so the easy option becomes the healthy one. And local advocacy gets health considered when transport routes, shops and open space are decided, when change is nearly free, not after. All four share one shape. Reach people where they are, change conditions instead of urging, and put the community inside the decision.

scenes.title: what transfers: the mechanism, not the activity

voiceover.text: So what can you take from another community? Use the transfer test from earlier, now for towns instead of countries. Step one, name the mechanism, not the activity. A community garden is an activity. Its mechanism might be food access, or social connection, or a reason for different groups to meet, or people feeling the space is theirs. Step two, can that mechanism work here? Is there a similar gap, a group to hold it, and a setting people use? Step three, what was local? A committed council, a long-standing organisation, one funder, one person. If it's missing here, it has to be built. Step four, check the population, and adapt it with the new community, not for them. Step five, decide what you'll measure before you start. So copy the mechanism, adapt the activity, rebuild what was local, and measure from day one.

scenes.title: why community-led works better, and its catch

voiceover.text: Here's why involving the community actually works. Community-led means the community sets the priorities and the design, not just comments on someone else's plan. Remember the ladder from Year 11: being consulted isn't leading. It finds the real problem: data shows a rate, but locals know the bus stops at six and the shop has closed. It's used, because people helped design it. It lasts, because the community owns it. And having control over decisions that affect your life is good for health in its own right. So the process is part of the intervention. But be honest about the catch. It's slower, it needs time and skills people may not have unpaid, and the loudest voices can take over. So it has to be community-led, properly resourced, and deliberate about including the people usually left out.
Two things to remember. Copy the mechanism, not the activity. And who decides is part of what works.

scenes.title: attempt one (a walking bus, and a sporting club)

voiceover.text: Two exam questions. First. Approach one: a walking school bus, where children walk to school in a supervised group. Approach two: a sporting club that becomes a place for health checks and mental health conversations. For each, name the likely mechanism, and what would have to be true in another community for it to transfer. Pause here to answer.

The walking bus builds daily activity into the trip to school. To transfer, the new town needs safe routes, schools within walking distance, and volunteers. The club works as a setting people already trust and visit, so it reaches people who'd never book a check. It needs strong clubs and trained people inside them. The classic mistake is naming the activity, not the mechanism.

Second. A state health department designs a youth mental health program in the capital, rolls it out unchanged to twenty country towns, and surveys each town after launch. Assess this approach using features of community approaches that work. Pause here to answer.

It fails the first line: who decided? The towns didn't set the priority, and a survey after launch is consultation, not leadership. It wasn't adapted to each population, and nothing local was rebuilt. It may not use settings young people already trust, or build local capacity. So it's likely to be weakly used and short-lived. The classic mistake is treating a survey as community-led.

So map the work to the four goals, run the strategy checklist, transfer the mechanism, and ask who decided. Now it's your turn. Turn those seven features into a blank planning sheet, for one community. How do you build a strategy for your own community, and show it may work before it starts?
